transcript.text: Indesit washer dryer washes fine but the drying cycle doesn't get warm at all, clothes come out cold and wet after 2 hours. Model is XWDE 96 something.

When a washer dryer washes fine but the drying is completely cold, the cause is almost always in the drying circuit, which is separate from the wash heater. On Indesit XWDE models, the usual suspects are:

1. Drying heater element (most common)
2. Thermal cutout / thermostat (one or more on the heater housing, often tripped or blown)
3. Drying fan motor (if it fails, the heater shuts off to prevent overheating)
4. Less often: wiring/connector burn-out at the heater, or a relay on the control board

## First, quick checks (no tools)

• Confirm you're actually selecting a dry cycle. On many XWDE models you have to press the drying button to set a time or dryness level. Wash-only programs won't dry.
• Listen during drying. Can you hear the fan whooshing, and does the drum turn back and forth?
• Fan running but cold air → points to the heater or a thermal cutout.
• No fan noise at all → points to the fan motor (or its wiring).
• Check the water supply. These are water-cooled condensers, so the cold tap must be on during drying. This affects efficiency, not heat, but it's worth ruling out.

## Find the full model number

Open the door and look on the sticker around the door frame. You'll need the full code (e.g., XWDE 961480X) to order the right parts, because elements and thermostats vary between versions.

## Testing the heater (if you're comfortable with a multimeter)

⚠️ Unplug the machine first, and turn off the water if you'll be moving it.

1. Remove the two screws at the back of the top lid, then slide the lid back and lift it off.
2. The drying heater sits in the fan/duct housing at the top, usually towards the back. It has a few wires and one or two small round thermostats attached.
3. Pull the connectors off and check resistance:
• Heater element: should read a value in the tens of ohms (roughly 20–60 Ω depending on model). Open circuit/infinite = dead element.
• Thermal cutouts/thermostats: should read near 0 Ω (continuity). Open = tripped or blown.
4. Some cutouts have a small reset button you can press. If it clicks, that may fix it temporarily. But a cutout usually trips for a reason, often a blocked air duct (lint build-up) or a failing fan, so clean the duct while you're in there.
5. Fan motor: spin the fan by hand to check it moves freely, and check the motor windings for continuity.

## Cost and practicality

• Heater elements and thermostats are usually cheap (roughly £15–£40 for aftermarket parts) and are a straightforward swap with basic tools.
• Indesit dryer heaters often come as an assembly with the thermostats already fitted. Buying it that way is usually easiest.
• If the heater, cutouts, and fan all test fine, the control board relay is the next suspect. That's more expensive and may be worth a repair engineer.

If you can tell me whether you hear the fan running during drying, and your full model number, I can help narrow it down further.
Yes, I can hear the fan whirring during drying and the drum is tumbling fine. The label on the door says XWDE 961480X W UK. No burning smell and nothing tripping either.

Since the fan runs and the drum tumbles, the motor and fan are fine. The fault is almost certainly in the drying heater circuit: the element, a thermal cutout, or the wiring to them. With no smell or tripping, the most likely cause is a blown thermal cutout or an open-circuit element.

## Most likely causes, in order

1. Thermal cutout (thermostat/thermal fuse) on the heater housing. This is very common on Indesit/Hotpoint washer dryers. There are usually two small round discs on the heater duct:
• One auto-reset thermostat that cycles the heat normally
• One one-shot safety cutout that blows permanently if the duct overheats. Some versions have a small reset button in the centre instead, so if you see one, press it firmly.
2. Drying heater element gone open-circuit
3. Burnt or loose spade connector at the heater (look for browned plastic or discoloured terminals)
4. Control board relay for the dryer heater (least likely, so check the parts above first)

## How to check (multimeter needed)

⚠️ Unplug the machine first.

1. Remove the two screws at the back of the top lid, slide it back, and lift it off.
2. The heater housing sits at the top of the machine. It's the duct the fan blows into, with the element terminals and the round thermostats mounted on it.
3. Take a photo of the wiring, then pull the connectors off one at a time and test:

| Part | Good reading | Faulty |
|---|---|---|
| Heater element | Roughly 25–60 Ω (some have two elements, so test each pair of terminals) | Open/infinite |
| Each thermostat/cutout | Near 0 Ω (continuity) | Open/infinite |

4. Inspect every connector and wire along that circuit for heat damage.

## Important: find out why it failed

If a cutout has blown, something usually made the duct overheat. The usual culprit is lint build-up in the fan housing or condenser duct. While the lid is off:
• Check the fan housing and the duct between the heater and drum for fluff and clean it out.
• Make sure the cold water supply is on during drying, because it cools the condenser.

If you skip this step, a new cutout can blow again quickly.

## Parts

Search using your full model number, XWDE 961480X W UK, on sites like eSpares, Partmaster, or Hotpoint/Indesit's official parts site. Heater elements and thermostat kits are model-specific and fairly inexpensive. Thermostats are often sold as a pair or kit with the element.

If you post your multimeter readings, I can help interpret them.
I don't have a multimeter, so I can't test continuity. I'm happy to unplug it and take the top off to have a look though. Is there anything I can check by eye?

Yes, there's a fair amount you can check by eye, though a blown cutout or broken element often looks perfectly normal. So if everything looks fine, that doesn't rule them out.

## Before you start

⚠️ Unplug the machine (don't just switch it off at the wall) and give it a while to cool if it's just been drying. The metal edges under the lid can be sharp, so gloves help.

1. Remove the two screws at the back of the top lid, slide it back about an inch, and lift it off.
2. Take a photo of everything before you touch anything, so you have a reference for the wiring.

## What to look for

1. Reset button on a thermostat
Find the small round metal discs on the heater/fan duct at the top. If any has a small button or pin in the centre, press it firmly. If it clicks, it had tripped, and that may be your fix. Run a dry cycle to test it, then still check for lint (step 5), as something made it trip.

2. Connectors and wiring
Follow the wires going to the heater terminals and thermostats. Look for:
• Brown, black or melted plastic on the spade connectors or plugs
• Discoloured (blue or dark) metal terminals
• Connectors that have slipped off or feel loose. Gently push each one back on firmly.
• Wires with cracked, brittle or scorched insulation

A burnt connector is a common fault and is easy to spot.

3. The heater element
On many models the element is hidden inside the duct, so you may only see its terminals. If you can see any of it, look for breaks, bulges or a blistered section in the coil or tube.

4. The thermostats themselves
Look for scorch marks, cracked casings or signs of heat around them. A one-shot cutout usually looks identical whether it's good or blown.

5. Lint build-up (worth doing regardless)
Look into the fan housing and the duct between the fan, heater and drum. A thick layer of fluff restricts airflow and is the classic reason cutouts blow. If you can, remove the duct cover and clear it out with a vacuum or soft brush.

## If nothing obvious shows up

You have three realistic options:

• Buy a cheap multimeter. A basic one costs about £10–15 from Screwfix, Toolstation, Amazon or similar. Testing the element and thermostats takes five minutes once the lid is off, and it means you only buy the part you actually need. This is the option I'd recommend.
• Replace the thermostats as a guess. They're inexpensive, often sold as a kit for this model, and they're the most common failure. The downside is that if it's actually the element, you've spent money without fixing it.
• Call an engineer. Choose this if you'd rather not go further.

When ordering any parts, search using XWDE 961480X W UK to make sure they fit.

If you spot something under the lid and you're not sure what it is, describe it or the markings on it and I can help you work out whether it looks like the problem.
Ok, I've had the top off. There's a heater box with wires on it and a small round button-like part on top, but I can't tell if it's blown. How would I know?

Honestly, you usually can't tell by looking. A blown thermal cutout looks identical to a working one. But there are a few things to try.

## 1. Check whether it's a reset type

Look closely at the centre of the round part:

• Small raised button or pin in the middle (sometimes under a little rubber cap you can flip off): this is a manual-reset thermostat. Press it firmly with your thumb or the blunt end of a pen.
• A click means it had tripped. Refit the lid and try a dry cycle.
• No click means it's either not tripped or not a reset type.
• Flat, sealed metal face with no button: it's either an auto-reset thermostat (resets itself when cool) or a one-shot cutout (fails permanently). There's nothing to press, and you can't see whether it's blown.

## 2. Look for a second cutout

There's often more than one. Check around the heater box, the fan housing and along the wires for:
• Another round disc
• A small cylindrical thermal fuse, sometimes inside a sleeve on one of the wires

Press any that have a button.

## 3. If pressing does nothing

At this point you can't narrow it down further by eye. You have three sensible options:

Option A: Get a cheap multimeter (recommended)
A basic one costs about £10–15 from Screwfix, Toolstation, Amazon or a supermarket. Use it like this:
1. Set it to the beep/continuity or lowest Ω setting.
2. Pull the two wires off the round part and touch a probe to each terminal.
3. A beep or near 0 Ω means it's fine. No beep means it's blown.
4. Then test the heater element terminals. Roughly 25–60 Ω is good. No reading means the element has failed.

This takes about 5 minutes and stops you buying the wrong part.

Option B: Buy the drying heater kit
For the XWDE 961480X, the drying heater is often sold as a kit with thermostats included. It costs roughly £25–50 from places like eSpares or Partmaster. Search using your full model number. It replaces the most likely failed parts in one go, but it costs more than guessing right with a meter.

Option C: Call an engineer
This is worth it if you'd rather not handle the wiring yourself.

## Two important points

• Don't bypass a cutout by joining the wires together. It's the only thing stopping the heater overheating and causing a fire.
• Clear any lint from the fan housing and duct while the top is off. If a cutout blew, fluff blocking the airflow is the usual reason, and a new one will blow again if it's left there.

If you can describe the round part in more detail, or tell me how many wires go to it, I can help you work out which type it is.

It's a small round part on top with no obvious button in the middle that I can tell, so I can't say if it's a reset type. I don't know how many wires go to it. Is there anything else I can check without a multimeter?

You've reached the limit of what you can tell by eye, but a few more checks are worth a couple of minutes.

## 1. Read the markings on the round part

Shine a torch on its face and sides. Thermostats usually have tiny printed or stamped text, such as:
• A temperature (e.g. "150°C" or "T150")
• A part or brand code (e.g. starting "KSD", or a manufacturer name)
• Sometimes "M" or "MAN" for manual reset

Take a close-up photo and zoom in, or search the code online. This often tells you whether it's manual-reset, auto-reset or one-shot.

## 2. Look again for a hidden reset

Some reset buttons are recessed or covered:
• A small hole in the centre that a pen tip or matchstick fits into. Press gently but firmly.
• A thin rubber or plastic cap you can flip off with a fingernail

## 3. Check the wires

You don't need to know the count in advance. Just look at where they connect:
• Usually two spade connectors push onto tabs on the thermostat, and two or more onto the heater box terminals.
• Push each connector firmly onto its tab. A loose one can stop the heater working.
• Look for browned, melted or blackened plastic, or dark or blue-tinged metal tabs. Check the connectors and the ends of the wires closely, as that's where burning usually shows.

## 4. Clear any lint

If you can see into the fan housing or duct, vacuum out any fluff. Even if it's not the cause now, it's the usual reason the cutout or heater fails, so it's worth doing before fitting any new part.

## If none of that turns anything up

You can't get any further without testing, so it comes down to the two options from before:

• £10–15 multimeter. The cheapest route. It tells you in five minutes whether it's the thermostat (a few pounds) or the element.
• Drying heater kit for the XWDE 961480X. Roughly £25–50, often including the thermostats. Enter your full model number on eSpares, Partmaster or similar to get the correct one. It fixes the most likely faults in one go without diagnosing.

If a new heater and thermostats don't fix it, the remaining suspect is the control board, and at that point an engineer is probably the better bet.
